claims.01-B1: Use HTTPS and the documented credential header. Reject query credentials. See REST Security.
claims.01-B2: Generate keys from 32 random bytes using a secure generator, such as secrets.token_urlsafe(32). See Python secrets.
claims.01-B3: Keep credentials out of logs and traces at every hop. Test rejection paths too. See Logging.
claims.01-B4: Use owned, scoped, expiring credential records and a secrets manager for caller storage. Test replacement and revocation separately from log prevention.
claims.01-B5: Check permissions after authentication; do not treat a valid key as unlimited access.
claims.01-O1: Use stronger caller authentication for higher-impact operations. Evaluate request signing in module 2, including its shared-secret limitations.

claims.02-S1: Use HMAC as RFC 2104 section 2 and FIPS 198-1 section 4 define it. FIPS 198-1 section 1 requires an approved hash function: "HMAC shall use an Approved cryptographic hash function". RFC 9421 section 3.3.3 defines HMAC with SHA-256.
claims.02-S2: Use a key at least as long as the hash output length L, which is 32 bytes for SHA-256. This is a recommendation, not a requirement: RFC 2104, an Informational RFC, says in section 2 that "the minimal recommended length for K is L bytes", and in section 3 it strongly discourages shorter keys.
claims.02-S3: Compare signatures with a constant-time function. The Python 3.14 documentation for the hmac module recommends hmac.compare_digest instead of == when verifying a digest, "to reduce the vulnerability to timing attacks". RFC 2104, FIPS 198-1 and RFC 9421 say nothing about comparison timing.
claims.02-B1: Sign method, host, path, query, timestamp, nonce, content type, and the SHA-256 of the raw body, in a documented fixed order.
claims.02-B2: Verify in this order: key lookup, time window, body hash, signature, nonce record. Record the nonce only after the signature verifies.
claims.02-B3: Accept timestamps within 5 minutes of server time. Keep nonces for at least the same period. Keep clocks synchronized.
claims.02-B4: Store keys in a secrets manager on both sides, versioned. Rotate with a short overlap in which both versions verify, then retire the old one.
claims.02-B5: Ensure proxies and gateways pass signed components through unchanged, or verify at the edge.
claims.02-O1: Use RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, with the content-digest field from RFC 9530, instead of a custom format.
claims.02-O2: Use asymmetric signatures when the receiver must not be able to forge caller requests.

claims.03-S1: Sign the signature base of RFC 9421 section 2.5, an ASCII string "containing the canonicalized HTTP message components covered by the signature", not a format of your own.
claims.03-S2: The @signature-params component is required as the last line of the signature base and must not be enumerated within the covered components of any signature, including itself. RFC 9421 section 2.3.
claims.03-S3: Carry the covered components and parameters in Signature-Input and the signature in Signature, both Dictionary structured fields. RFC 9421 sections 4.1 and 4.2.
claims.03-S4: RFC 9421 section 2.3 defines the value of the alg parameter as an algorithm from the HTTP Signature Algorithms registry. Section 6.2.2 lists its initial contents, which include ed25519, ecdsa-p256-sha256 and rsa-pss-sha512.
claims.03-S5: RFC 9421 section 1.4 requires an application or profile to specify, at a minimum, the set of component identifiers and signature parameters that are expected and required, a means of retrieving key material, the "set of allowable signature algorithms to be used by signers and accepted by verifiers", a "means of determining that the signature algorithm used to verify the signature is appropriate for the key material and context of the message", and the errors returned when validation fails, among other items. Write these down before you implement.
claims.03-S6: To protect the body, cover a digest of it. RFC 9421 section 1 states that the specification "does not define a means to directly cover HTTP message content", and section 7.2.8 that a digest field from RFC 9530 "can be included just like any other field", so the body is only protected by covering a digest field that describes it.
claims.03-S7: Treat anything outside the covered components as untrusted. RFC 9421 section 7.2.1 says "The verifier should only trust message components that have been signed", because portions not covered are "susceptible to modification by an attacker without affecting the signature".
claims.03-S8: Compute Content-Digest as defined in RFC 9530 section 2, using an algorithm whose status is Active, which section 5 recommends. The initial registry contents in section 7.2 list two: sha-512 and sha-256.
claims.03-S9: For ecdsa-p256-sha256 the signature value is R followed by S, each zero-padded to 32 octets (RFC 9421 section 3.3.4), not a DER encoding.
claims.03-B1: Verify in this order: resolve keyid, check alg against the allowlist, check alg against the key, check required coverage, rebuild the base, verify the signature, recompute the digest, check created and expires, record the nonce.
claims.03-B2: Recompute the digest from the received bytes on every request. Covering content-digest without recomputing it protects the header and not the body.
claims.03-B3: Accept a created value within 300 seconds of server time in either direction, and document that number as the replay window for anything you do not record.
claims.03-B4: Require a nonce, record it only after the signature verifies, and store it where every instance serving the endpoint can see it.
claims.03-B5: Resolve keyid only against keys established out of band. Never fetch key material from a location the caller supplies.
claims.03-B6: Issue a new keyid for every key and accept both during a rotation overlap.
claims.03-O1: Keep an HMAC where both parties are the same organisation, there is one receiver, and no request will ever need attributing to one side. RFC 9421's hmac-sha256 lets you do that inside the same format.
claims.03-O2: Sign responses as well as requests, and bind a response to its request, where a client needs to prove what it was told. RFC 9421 supports both directions.
claims.03-O3: Hold the private key in a hardware-backed or non-exportable keystore, which is what makes the last row of the attack table hard rather than merely unlikely.

claims.04-S1: Public clients must use PKCE, and authorization servers must support it. For confidential clients RFC 9700 section 2.1.1 recommends it rather than requiring it.
claims.04-S2: A client that can use S256 must use S256. RFC 7636 section 4.2 makes S256 mandatory to implement on the server, and section 7.2 says plain should not be used.
claims.04-S3: The code verifier is 43 to 128 characters from the unreserved set, generated with a high-entropy cryptographic random source. RFC 7636 section 4.1.
claims.04-S4: Authorization servers must match redirect URIs by exact string comparison, except for port numbers in localhost redirect URIs of native apps. RFC 9700 section 2.1.
claims.04-S5: A client must not use an authorization code more than once. On reuse the server must deny the request and should revoke tokens previously issued from that code. RFC 6749 section 4.1.2, which also recommends a maximum code lifetime of 10 minutes.
claims.04-S6: The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used. RFC 9700 section 2.4.
claims.04-S7: RFC 9700 section 2.1.2 says clients should not use the implicit grant, or any response type that returns an access token in the authorization response, unless access token injection in the authorization response is prevented and the token leakage vectors that section names are mitigated.
claims.04-S8: For the client credentials grant, a refresh token should not be included in the response. RFC 6749 section 4.4.3.
claims.04-S9: Send bearer tokens in the Authorization header. RFC 6750 section 2.1 says clients should use it and resource servers must support it.
claims.04-S10: Token endpoint errors use the codes defined in RFC 6749 section 5.2 with HTTP 400 unless specified otherwise: invalid_request, invalid_client, invalid_grant, unauthorized_client, unsupported_grant_type, invalid_scope.
claims.04-B1: Verify the challenge with the method recorded at the authorization request. Ignore any method supplied at redemption.
claims.04-B2: One client registration per application and environment, with its own redirect URIs and its own narrow scope list.
claims.04-B3: Issue codes with a 60 second lifetime. The legitimate client redeems immediately; a long lifetime only helps an attacker.
claims.04-B4: Resource servers check the audience first, then the scope for the specific operation, then object-level authorization.
claims.04-B5: Error responses name the RFC 6749 error code and nothing about which check failed.
claims.04-O1: Sender-constrain access tokens with mTLS (RFC 8705) or DPoP (RFC 9449) where token theft is a material risk. RFC 9700 section 2.2.1 recommends this rather than requiring it. Module 7.
claims.04-O2: Use a backend for frontend so a browser application's tokens are held server side and never reach page scripts.
claims.04-O3: Add OpenID Connect when the client needs standardized user authentication rather than delegated access. Module 35.

claims.05-S1: The caller must be able to specify a supported set of algorithms, and no others may be used. RFC 8725 section 3.1, which also requires that the alg header specifies the same algorithm actually used.
claims.05-S2: Applications must only allow cryptographically current algorithms that meet their security requirements. RFC 8725 section 3.2.
claims.05-S3: Implementations must not accept Unsecured JWSs, the alg value none, by default, and applications must not signal acceptance of them at a global level. RFC 7518 section 3.6.
claims.05-S4: When a JWT contains iss, the application must validate that the keys used belong to that issuer, and must reject the JWT if they do not. RFC 8725 section 3.8.
claims.05-S5: Where one issuer can issue JWTs for more than one relying party, the audience value must be validated, and the JWT rejected if the audience is absent or not associated with the recipient. RFC 8725 section 3.9. RFC 7519 section 4.1.3 says that when aud is present, the JWT must be rejected if the principal is not identified by a value in it.
claims.05-S6: Where one issuer can issue more than one kind of JWT, the validation rules must be mutually exclusive and reject JWTs of the wrong kind. RFC 8725 section 3.12. Explicit typing is covered in section 3.11.
claims.05-S7: The current time must be before exp. RFC 7519 section 4.1.4, which allows a small leeway for clock skew.
claims.05-S8: An OAuth JWT access token requires iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti, and RFC 9068 section 2.1 requires the typ header to carry the access token media type, recommending the short form at+jwt. Section 4 requires the resource server to reject a token whose typ is neither at+jwt nor application/at+jwt. Under RFC 9068 section 2.2, a client credentials token still has sub, and the RFC recommends that it identify the client rather than a user.
claims.05-B1: Declare the whole profile in configuration: algorithms, type, issuer, audience, required claims, key source and leeway. Read none of it from the token.
claims.05-B2: Verify in this order: algorithm allowlist, token type, signature, required claims present, then claim values. Reject before reading anything you have not yet authenticated.
claims.05-B3: Select the key from the issuer's published key set by kid. Never follow jku or x5u from the token header.
claims.05-B4: Allow 60 seconds of clock leeway in both directions, and document it.
claims.05-B5: Return 401 with no indication of which check failed. Log the specific reason with a correlation ID.
claims.05-O1: Use a reviewed JWT library rather than writing the parsing yourself, and configure its algorithm, audience and issuer options explicitly, because most default to checking less than this list.
claims.05-O2: Sender-constrain the token with mTLS or DPoP where theft is a material risk. Module 7.

claims.06-S1: A JWK Set is a JSON object that must have a keys member whose value is an array of JWKs. RFC 7517 section 5.
claims.06-S2: A server providing a jwks_uri endpoint shall serve it only over TLS. FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2.
claims.06-S3: RFC 7517 section 4.5 recommends that different keys within a set use distinct kid values, and FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 recommends against serving a set with multiple keys sharing a kid. Both are recommendations, not requirements.
claims.06-S4: FAPI 2.0 section 5.4.2 recommends against using the jku and x5u JOSE headers.
claims.06-S5: The use parameter indicates whether a public key is for encryption or for verifying signatures. RFC 7517 section 4.2. The alg parameter is OPTIONAL, section 4.4.
claims.06-S6: A revocation endpoint returns HTTP 200 whether the token was revoked or was already invalid, because "invalid tokens do not cause an error response since the client cannot handle such an error in a reasonable way". RFC 7009 section 2.2.
claims.06-S7: Where the authorization server supports revoking access tokens, RFC 7009 section 2.1 recommends that revoking a refresh token also invalidates the access tokens issued from the same grant, and warns that "there could be a propagation delay, for example, in which some servers know about the invalidation while others do not".
claims.06-S8: The introspection active member is a "Boolean indicator of whether or not the presented token is currently active". RFC 7662 section 2.2.
claims.06-S9: An introspection response may be cached "at the cost of liveness of the information used by the protected resource to make authorization decisions" (RFC 7662 section 2.2), and a response carrying exp must not be cached beyond it (section 4).
claims.06-B1: Refresh the key set on a schedule once it passes a maximum age, independently of whether any kid is missing.
claims.06-B2: On an unknown kid, allow one bounded refresh, coalesce concurrent misses into a single fetch, and apply a cooldown so caller-supplied identifiers cannot drive a fetch storm.
claims.06-B3: After a failed refresh attempt, make no other attempt until a back-off has passed. Time it from the failure and track it separately from the last successful load, so a failing endpoint is not fetched on every request and a healthy one is still refreshed on schedule.
claims.06-B4: A successful, well formed key set is authoritative even when it contains zero usable signing keys. It replaces what you hold.
claims.06-B5: A malformed, truncated, non-success or transport-failed refresh is not authoritative. Keep the last known good set, and fail the request that required the refresh. Keep serving the kept set while the endpoint is down, up to the staleness limit, and count the outage and one back-off in the revocation bound.
claims.06-B6: Set a hard limit on staleness. Once the last successful load is as old as the limit, serve no key from the set and reject every token with a distinct reason until a refresh succeeds, still retrying at the back-off rate. This fails closed: a removed key cannot outlast the limit, and a longer outage of the key endpoint rejects every caller.
claims.06-B7: Run the scheduled refresh from a background task as well as on requests, with the same back-off, so the last successful load stays within about one maximum age on an API with no traffic. An outage then starts with at least the staleness limit less one maximum age still to run. The cost is one fetch per maximum age from every verifier instance, whatever the traffic. It does not shorten the worst case for a removed key during an outage.
claims.06-B8: Reject a kid that matches more than one eligible key rather than selecting by array order, and report it as an issuer fault.
claims.06-B9: State the revocation bound as a sum of the token lifetime and every cache TTL on the path, and test it by disabling an account and timing the result.
claims.06-O1: Use introspection or a denylist at the resource server when the revocation bound must be shorter than the token lifetime. The cost is a live dependency on the authorization server.
claims.06-O2: Serve the stale key set with a much longer limit, or none, where rejecting every caller is the worse failure and the path to the key endpoint is hard for an attacker to block. The cost is that a removed key verifies for as long as the endpoint is unreachable. Write that into the revocation bound and alert on the outage.
claims.06-O3: Use short token lifetimes instead, accepting that the bound cannot go below one lifetime and that the authorization server sees more traffic.

claims.07-S1: When a certificate-bound access token is represented as a JWT, the certificate hash should be represented using the x5t#S256 confirmation method, a base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash of the DER encoding of the X.509 certificate. The value must omit padding and must not include line breaks or whitespace. RFC 8705 section 3.1.
claims.07-S2: A protected resource must obtain the client certificate from its TLS implementation layer and must verify it matches the certificate associated with the access token, rejecting a mismatch with HTTP 401 and invalid_token. RFC 8705 section 3.
claims.07-S3: A DPoP proof JWT must carry typ of dpop+jwt and the claims jti, htm, htu and iat. RFC 9449 section 4.2.
claims.07-S4: When a DPoP proof accompanies an access token it must carry ath, the base64url SHA-256 hash of the ASCII encoding of that token. RFC 9449 section 4.2.
claims.07-S5: The jkt confirmation value must be the base64url encoding of the JWK SHA-256 thumbprint of the DPoP public key. RFC 9449 section 6.1, using the thumbprint of RFC 7638.
claims.07-S6: A resource server must check that a DPoP proof was received, check it according to RFC 9449 section 4.3, and check that its public key matches the key the access token is bound to. RFC 9449 section 7.1.
claims.07-S7: Servers must only accept DPoP proofs for a limited time after creation, "preferably only for a relatively brief period on the order of seconds or minutes". RFC 9449 section 11.1.
claims.07-S8: RFC 9700 section 2.2.1 recommends that authorization and resource servers use mechanisms for sender-constraining access tokens. It is a recommendation, not a requirement.
claims.07-B1: Record every accepted proof jti for at least the proof time window, in a store shared across every instance serving the endpoint, and record it only after all other checks pass.
claims.07-B2: Accept proofs within 60 seconds of server time in either direction, and document that number as the replay window for anything you fail to record.
claims.07-B3: Terminate mutual TLS where the binding check happens. If a certificate must be forwarded in a header, treat that header as a credential and prove no other path can set it.
claims.07-B4: A bound token presented without its proof or certificate fails. Never fall back to bearer behaviour when the binding material is absent.
claims.07-B5: Keep audience, scope and object-level authorization exactly as they were. Binding answers who is calling, not what they may do.
claims.07-O1: Use a DPoP nonce supplied by the server where you need to constrain proof creation time more tightly than a clock window allows. RFC 9449 defines the mechanism.
claims.07-O2: Store the client private key in a hardware-backed or non-exportable keystore, which is what converts binding from a token-theft control into a meaningful one.

claims.08-S1: NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5 section 2.1 defines a cryptoperiod as "the time span during which a specific key is authorized for use or in which the keys for a given system or application may remain in effect", and section 5.3 says the risk and consequences of exposure "should be carefully considered when selecting the cryptoperiod". This module treats the active life of a credential as one.
claims.08-S2: Carry the lifecycle through to an end state. NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5 section 8.3.4 requires that all copies of a private or secret key "shall be destroyed as soon as they are no longer required". Section 2.1 says a key reaches the destroyed state when it is destroyed, and that although the key no longer exists, "its previous existence may be recorded (e.g., in metadata or audit logs)".
claims.08-S3: The client credentials grant "MUST only be used by confidential clients", so a credential used with it belongs to a component that can keep a secret. RFC 6749 section 4.4, with section 2.1 on the confidential and public client distinction.
claims.08-S4: Prefer asymmetric client authentication. RFC 9700 section 2.5 recommends mutual TLS or a signed JWT over a client secret, because then "authorization servers do not need to store sensitive symmetric keys, making these methods more robust against leakage of keys".
claims.08-S5: Where workload identity is available, a SPIFFE ID is "an RFC 3986 compliant URI comprising a 'trust domain name' and an associated path", carried as a URI entry in the certificate's Subject Alternative Name extension, and an X.509 SVID "MUST contain exactly one URI SAN". SPIFFE-ID specification section 2 and X509-SVID specification section 2.
claims.08-S6: Do not read more into a trust domain than it carries. The SPIFFE-ID specification, section 2.1.1, states there is "no centralized authority for regulation or registration of trust domain names".
claims.08-B1: Every credential record carries six facts: owner as a team, purpose and scope, rotation interval with last-rotated date, retirement condition, revocation route, and last used.
claims.08-B2: The register holds metadata only. Never the secret value.
claims.08-B3: Rotate shared secrets every 90 days and asymmetric signing keys every 365, with the successor published before the cutover, and record a reason for any interval you lengthen.
claims.08-B4: Issue one credential per system. A credential two systems share is the one that never gets rotated.
claims.08-B5: Withdraw an active credential unused for more than 90 days, or record why it is kept.
claims.08-B6: Reconcile the register against the deployment monthly, reading the systems, and report both directions of the difference.
claims.08-B7: Revoke first, confirm the credential is refused, then remove the record. Never the other order.
claims.08-B8: Publish the date of the last reconciliation and the count of unknowns beside any statement that the estate is clean.
claims.08-O1: Replace static secrets with platform-issued workload identities where they are available, which converts a rotation problem into a question about the issuing infrastructure.
claims.08-O2: Issue a distinct credential per agent instance or per task where the platform allows it, so that the blast radius of one is not the whole fleet.

claims.19-S1: Token exchange uses the grant type urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange. RFC 8693 section 2.1.
claims.19-S2: Impersonation makes principal A "indistinguishable from B in that context"; with delegation, A "still has its own identity separate from B" and "any actions taken are being taken by A representing B". RFC 8693 section 1.1.
claims.19-S3: grant_type, subject_token and subject_token_type are REQUIRED. actor_token_type "is REQUIRED when the actor_token parameter is present in the request but MUST NOT be included otherwise". RFC 8693 section 2.1.
claims.19-S4: audience, resource, scope and requested_token_type are OPTIONAL, and no lifetime limit is specified. RFC 8693 section 2.1.
claims.19-S5: The response carries access_token, issued_token_type and token_type as REQUIRED; scope is "OPTIONAL if the scope of the issued security token is identical to the scope requested by the client; otherwise, it is REQUIRED". RFC 8693 section 2.2.1.
claims.19-S6: "If the issued token is not an access token or usable as an access token, then the token_type value N_A is used to indicate that an OAuth 2.0 token_type identifier is not applicable in that context." RFC 8693 section 2.2.1.
claims.19-S7: An invalid request, or a subject_token or actor_token that is invalid or "unacceptable based on policy", MUST return the invalid_request error code; invalid_target SHOULD be used when the server is unwilling or unable to issue for the requested target. The section adds: "Other error codes may also be used, as appropriate." RFC 8693 section 2.2.2, with the error response format and codes from RFC 6749 section 5.2.
claims.19-S8: "The outermost act claim represents the current actor while nested act claims represent prior actors." RFC 8693 section 4.1.
claims.19-S9: "For the purpose of applying access control policy, the consumer of a token MUST only consider the token's top-level claims and the party identified as the current actor by the act claim." RFC 8693 section 4.1.
claims.19-S10: The may_act claim "makes a statement that one party is authorized to become the actor and act on behalf of another party", and "can be used by the authorization server to determine whether the client (or party identified in the actor_token) is authorized to engage in the requested delegation or impersonation". RFC 8693 section 4.4.
claims.19-S11: "The use of the scope claim (in addition to other typical constraints such as a limited token lifetime) is suggested to mitigate potential for such abuse, as it restricts the contexts in which the delegated rights can be exercised." RFC 8693 section 5.
claims.19-S12: ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse "exploits dynamic trust and delegation in agents to escalate access and bypass controls by manipulating delegation chains, role inheritance, control flows, and agent context". OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026, ASI03.
claims.19-B1: Exchange rather than forward. A user's token does not leave the audience it was issued for.
claims.19-B2: Send actor_token, so the downstream decision and the audit record name the agent and the user separately.
claims.19-B3: Require audience and scope on every exchange at the authorization server, rather than defaulting to the subject token's scope.
claims.19-B4: Enforce may_act, matched on issuer and subject together.
claims.19-B5: Cap the issued lifetime at the subject token's remaining life.
claims.19-B6: Authorize on the current actor only, and bound the depth of chains you accept.
claims.19-B7: Log the subject and the current actor on every delegated call.
claims.19-O1: Bind the issued token to its holder with the mechanisms in module 7 where a stolen bearer token is in the threat model.
claims.19-O2: Issue impersonation tokens where a downstream service must not learn that an agent is involved, recording the decision and accepting that attribution is lost.
claims.19-O3: Keep an exchange record per issued token, so a revoked session can be traced to the tokens minted from it even though it cannot recall them.

claims.27-S1: OWASP API2:2023 Broken Authentication, an awareness document that sets no requirements, recommends treating credential recovery endpoints as login endpoints for brute force, rate limiting and lockout; re-authentication for sensitive operations; multi-factor authentication where possible; anti-brute-force mechanisms stricter than the regular rate limiting; account lockout or CAPTCHA; and weak-password checks. OWASP API2:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.27-S2: The OWASP Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet calls multi-factor authentication "by far the best defense against the majority of password-related attacks, including credential stuffing and password spraying", and says blocking IP addresses "should not be used as the sole or primary defense". Credential Stuffing Prevention Cheat Sheet, Multi-Factor Authentication and IP Mitigation and Intelligence.
claims.27-S3: The OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet, which is guidance and sets no requirements, says that for login, password reset and password recovery "an application must respond with a generic error message" whether the user ID or password was wrong, the account does not exist, or the account is locked or disabled, and warns that a different HTTP status code or processing time leaks the same thing. Authentication Cheat Sheet, Authentication and Error Messages.
claims.27-S4: The same cheat sheet recommends that the counter of failed logins be associated with the account and not the source IP address, and that a lockout design take care not to let an attacker deny service by locking other users' accounts. Authentication Cheat Sheet, Account Lockout.
claims.27-S5: For the systems it covers, NIST requires a verifier to limit consecutive failed attempts on one account to no more than 100, allows lower limits, allows a wait that grows as the account nears its limit, and recommends disregarding earlier failures after a successful authentication. NIST SP 800-63B-4 section 3.2.2.
claims.27-S6: For the systems it covers, NIST requires a minimum of 15 characters for a password used as the only factor and 8 when it is only used with another factor, recommends allowing at least 64, forbids other composition rules and scheduled changes, and requires each new password to be compared in full with a blocklist of commonly used, expected or compromised values, with the reason given on rejection. NIST SP 800-63B-4 section 3.1.1.2.
claims.27-S7: For the systems it covers, NIST requires stored passwords to be salted and hashed with a suitable password hashing scheme, with a salt of at least 32 bits, and recommends a cost factor as high as practical and a further keyed hash whose key is stored separately. NIST SP 800-63B-4 section 3.1.1.2.
claims.27-S8: The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet recommends Argon2id with a minimum of 19 MiB of memory, an iteration count of 2 and 1 degree of parallelism; scrypt with a cost parameter of at least 2^17, block size 8 and parallelization 1 if Argon2id is not available; bcrypt with a work factor of 10 or more for legacy systems; and PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA-256 and 600,000 or more iterations if FIPS-140 compliance is required. Password Storage Cheat Sheet, Introduction.
claims.27-S9: The OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet recommends a consistent message and a uniform response time for existing and non-existing accounts; tokens that are randomly generated with a cryptographically safe algorithm, long enough to resist brute force, stored securely, single use, expiring and linked to an individual user; no change to the account until a valid token is presented; and no account lockout in response to a forgotten password attack. Forgot Password Cheat Sheet, Introduction, General Security Practices and Account Lockout.
claims.27-S10: For the systems it covers, NIST requires a recovery code that is issued to an address to be valid for at most 24 hours when sent by email and 10 minutes when sent by text message or voice, requires its verification to be throttled, and requires a notification to the subscriber whenever an account is recovered. NIST SP 800-63B-4 section 4.2.
claims.27-S11: The 429 (Too Many Requests) status code "indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time". The response may include a Retry-After header and must not be stored by a cache. A server is not required to use 429. RFC 6585 sections 4 and 7.2.
claims.27-S12: A server that generates a 401 (Unauthorized) response must send a WWW-Authenticate header field with at least one challenge. RFC 9110 sections 15.5.2 and 11.6.1. The lab models status and message only.
claims.27-S13: RFC 6238, an Informational RFC, recommends a default time step of 30 seconds and at most one time step of allowance for network delay, and says a verifier "MUST NOT accept the second attempt of the OTP after the successful validation has been issued for the first OTP". RFC 4226, also Informational, recommends throttling one-time password validation at the server. RFC 6238 section 5.2 and RFC 4226 section 7.3.
claims.27-B1: Count failed attempts both per submitted username and per source, and check both before any password hash is computed. Count attempts, not requests, so a batch of ten logins in one request is ten attempts.
claims.27-B2: Lock for a short period that grows with each further failure up to a fixed cap. Do not count attempts refused during a lock. Clear the count on a successful sign-in or reset.
claims.27-B3: For an unknown account, verify against a dummy record and count the failure, so the status, the body, the work and the eventual 429 are the same as for a real account.
claims.27-B4: Generate reset tokens with 32 bytes from a cryptographic generator, store only a hash, tie each to one account, expire it after 15 minutes, delete it on use, and let a new request replace the old token.
claims.27-B5: After a reset, end the account's sessions, notify the user and require a normal sign-in.
claims.27-B6: Require the current password or a second factor to change the sign-in address, the password or the second factor, and notify the previous address.
claims.27-B7: Log every failure, lockout and reset, and alert on the patterns: many accounts from one source, and many sources against one account. Module 30 (Logging, detection and response) covers what to do with them.
claims.27-O1: Require a CAPTCHA after a few failures. The Authentication Cheat Sheet treats it as defence in depth that makes guessing slower and more expensive, not as prevention.
claims.27-O2: Ask for the second factor only when a sign-in looks unusual: a new device, an unusual location, an address that has tried several accounts.
claims.27-O3: Offer phishing-resistant authenticators such as passkeys. For the systems it covers, NIST requires a verifier to offer at least one phishing-resistant option at authentication assurance level 2 (section 2.2.2).
claims.27-O4: Do not build it. OWASP A07:2025 suggests using a premade, well-trusted system for authentication, identity and session management where possible. The checklist below then becomes the list of questions to ask about that system.

claims.35-S1: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 requires a client to validate the ID token. The issuer identifier "MUST exactly match the value of the iss (issuer) Claim". The client must validate that aud contains its client_id, and the token "MUST be rejected if the ID Token does not list the Client as a valid audience, or if it contains additional audiences not trusted by the Client". "The current time MUST be before the time represented by the exp Claim." If a nonce was sent, the claim must be present and must be checked to be the same value.
claims.35-S2: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 states these at lower strength. The alg should be RS256 or the algorithm the client registered. The client should check the nonce for replay, should check that a requested acr is appropriate, and should check a requested auth_time. Checking that azp is its own client_id is something the validation may include. iat "can be used" to reject old tokens, with no requirement.
claims.35-S3: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 3.1.3.7 allows TLS server validation in place of the signature check for an ID token received directly from the token endpoint, and requires the client to validate the signature of all other ID tokens, using keys provided by the issuer. Sections 3.2.2.11 and 3.3.2.12 require the signature check, and section 3.2.2.11 the nonce check, for an ID token from the authorization endpoint.
claims.35-S4: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 2 forbids none as the ID token alg unless the response type returns no ID token from the authorization endpoint and the client explicitly requested none at registration. Section 10.1 says the MAC key is the octets of the UTF-8 representation of the client_secret and that symmetric signatures must not be used by public clients. Section 16.19 requires at least 32 octets of client_secret for HS256. Section 15.1 requires providers to support RS256, with the exception it states.
claims.35-S5: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 sections 3.2.2.10 and 3.3.2.11 require the provider to include at_hash when an ID token is issued from the authorization endpoint with an access token, and c_hash when it is issued there with a code. Sections 3.2.2.9 and 3.3.2.10 say the client should validate them. In the code flow section 3.1.3.6 makes at_hash optional and section 3.1.3.8 says the client may use it.
claims.35-S6: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 section 5.3.2 requires that the sub in the UserInfo response "MUST be verified to exactly match the sub Claim in the ID Token; if they do not match, the UserInfo Response values MUST NOT be used". Section 5.7 says only iss and sub together identify a user and that claims such as email must not be used as unique identifiers.
claims.35-S7: OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 section 4.3 requires the issuer in the configuration document to be identical to the issuer URL used to retrieve it, and to the iss of ID tokens from that issuer. Section 7.2 requires the relying party to ensure all three match exactly, and to perform TLS certificate checking on the configuration request.
claims.35-S8: RFC 9068 section 2.1 requires JWT access tokens to carry the application/at+jwt media type in typ, and says the value used should be at+jwt. Section 4 requires the resource server to verify that the header value is at+jwt or application/at+jwt and to "reject tokens carrying any other value", and to reject a token whose aud does not name it. Section 6 says the client must not inspect the access token.
claims.35-S9: RFC 8725 section 2.8 requires mitigations where a JWT "could be confused with other kinds of JWTs". Section 3.12 requires validation rules for different kinds of JWT from one issuer to be mutually exclusive. Section 3.11 recommends explicit typing for new uses of JWTs.
claims.35-S10: RFC 9700 section 2.1.1 requires clients to prevent authorization code injection: public clients must use PKCE, PKCE is recommended for confidential clients, and a confidential OpenID Connect client may use nonce in its place. Either value must be transaction-specific and bound to the client and the user agent. Section 4.5.3.2 sets the two conditions for relying on nonce. Section 4.4.2 requires a client that uses more than one authorization server to store the issuer of each authorization request.
claims.35-S11: RFC 9700 section 2.1.2 says clients should not use the implicit grant or other response types that issue access tokens in the authorization response, unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage it names is mitigated. RFC 10017 section 7.2 requires, for browser-based applications, that the authorization server issue access tokens only from the token endpoint and that clients not use the implicit grant to obtain access tokens.
claims.35-S12: Draft, not a standard: draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-16 omits the implicit grant, and says in section 10.1 that removing response_type=token does not affect extension response types such as response_type=id_token.
claims.35-B1: An API accepts only access tokens issued for it. A client accepts only ID tokens issued for it, validates them once at the callback, and never forwards one.
claims.35-B2: Fix the ID token algorithm at registration and compare the header with it before anything else. Validate the signature of every ID token, including those from the token endpoint. Never register none.
claims.35-B3: Send a fresh nonce with every authentication request, derived from a random value kept in the browser session, together with PKCE and state. Use no token until the nonce comparison has passed.
claims.35-B4: Trust no additional audience, and reject an azp that is not this client. Refuse an ID token issued more than 10 minutes ago. Allow 60 seconds of clock leeway.
claims.35-B5: Beside a token or code from a redirect, treat a missing at_hash or c_hash as a rejection.
claims.35-B6: Key user accounts on iss and sub. Run the client's own session with its own timeouts, and ask the provider again before a sensitive step.
claims.35-B7: Configure the issuer URL. Do not derive it from user input.
claims.35-O1: HS256 ID tokens for a confidential client, where the client holding the signing key is acceptable and the secret is random and at least 32 octets.
claims.35-O2: The hybrid response type code id_token, where a profile requires an ID token in the authorization response. Validate its signature, nonce and c_hash, and then the ID token from the token endpoint as well.
claims.35-O3: Relying on TLS in place of the signature for an ID token read directly from the token endpoint, which Core allows. Choose it only if no other path can reach the same validator.

modules.title: Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth

claims.36-S1: RFC 9700 section 2.5 recommends asymmetric cryptography for client authentication, such as mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or signed JWTs (private_key_jwt), and says authorization servers should enforce client authentication where issuing and protecting client credentials is feasible.
claims.36-S2: The client must not use more than one authentication method in a request. RFC 6749 section 2.3. The server must not rely on public client authentication to identify the client. Same section.
claims.36-S3: A JWT used for client authentication must contain iss, sub equal to the client_id, an aud that identifies the authorization server, and exp, and must be signed or carry a MAC. The server must reject one with an invalid signature or MAC, one that does not name it as audience, and one that has expired. RFC 7523 section 3. Failures are reported as invalid_client. RFC 7523 section 3.2.
claims.36-S4: RFC 7523 section 3 allows, and does not require, a jti claim and replay tracking. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2, section 9, requires jti for private_key_jwt and client_secret_jwt and requires that the assertion be used only once unless the parties negotiated otherwise.
claims.36-S5: For JWT client authentication the client should use the authorization server's issuer identifier as the audience, and the server must accept its issuer identifier, its token endpoint URL or its PAR endpoint URL. RFC 9126 section 2.
claims.36-S6: The PAR endpoint must authenticate the client as the token endpoint does, must reject a pushed request that contains request_uri, and must validate the request as it would an authorization request. RFC 9126 section 2.1.
claims.36-S7: The request_uri must contain a part generated with a cryptographically strong pseudorandom algorithm so that guessing a valid value is computationally infeasible, and must be bound to the client that posted the request. RFC 9126 section 2.2.
claims.36-S8: An expired request_uri must be rejected. The server should treat request_uri values as one-time use and may allow a duplicate caused by a reload. The client must use a value only once. RFC 9126 section 4.
claims.36-S9: Server policy may make PAR the only way to pass authorization request data, globally or per client, signalled by require_pushed_authorization_requests. The server then refuses other authorization requests with invalid_request. RFC 9126 sections 4, 5 and 6.
claims.36-S10: The server must accept new redirect URIs in a pushed request only from authenticated clients. RFC 9126 section 7.2. Clients should use PKCE, a unique state or the OpenID Connect nonce against request URI swapping. RFC 9126 section 7.5.
claims.36-S11: Each authorization_details object requires a type. The server must refuse an unknown type, unknown fields, fields of the wrong type, invalid values and missing required fields, with invalid_authorization_details. RFC 9396 sections 2 and 5.
claims.36-S12: The token response must return the authorization_details as granted, and the authorization server must make them available to the resource server. RFC 9396 sections 7 and 9.
claims.36-S13: If the integrity of authorization_details is a concern, clients must protect them against tampering and swapping, with a signed request object or with PAR. The server must sanitize the data to prevent injection. RFC 9396 section 12.
claims.36-S14: A resource server signals that the authentication behind a token is not sufficient with the error code insufficient_user_authentication, and may state the requirement with acr_values, max_age or both. RFC 9470 section 3. The client should use those values in a new authorization request. RFC 9470 section 4.
claims.36-S15: The authorization server should treat a requested acr as necessary when issuing the access token, and fail the request if it cannot be met. RFC 9470 section 5. RFC 9470 must not be used to position OAuth as an authentication protocol. RFC 9470 section 9.
claims.36-S16: The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used. RFC 9700 section 2.4. Clients should not use the implicit grant or other response types that return an access token in the authorization response, unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage vectors that section names are mitigated. RFC 9700 section 2.1.2.
claims.36-S17: A client that can interact with more than one authorization server is required to have a defense against mix-up attacks, and should use the iss parameter of RFC 9207 or an equivalent issuer value in the response. RFC 9700 section 2.1. A client that supports RFC 9207 must compare iss with the issuer of the server the request was sent to and reject a mismatch. RFC 9207 section 2.4.
claims.36-S18: Under the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile, authorization servers shall authenticate clients with mutual TLS or private_key_jwt, shall reject authorization requests sent without PAR, shall require PKCE with S256, shall return iss, shall issue only sender-constrained access tokens, and shall reject the password grant. FAPI 2.0 Security Profile sections 5.3.2.1 and 5.3.2.2. Resource servers shall verify the token and that the authorization it represents is sufficient. Section 5.3.4.
claims.36-B1: Register private_key_jwt for every confidential client. Accept one audience, the issuer identifier. Cap the assertion lifetime and record each jti until exp, after the signature and claims have passed.
claims.36-B2: Take the assertion's algorithm and key from the client's registration, never from the JWT header.
claims.36-B3: Require PAR for every client whose request parameters matter. Use only what was pushed, and ignore anything else on the authorization URL.
claims.36-B4: Put anything with an amount, a payee or a named object in authorization_details. At the API, compare every field of the granted object with the request. Build the consent text from the same object.
claims.36-B5: Validate the token before applying the step-up policy, so that an invalid token is not told what the policy is.
claims.36-B6: Treat a profile claim as a list to verify row by row, and test object-level authorization separately.
claims.36-O1: Mutual TLS client authentication (tls_client_auth or self_signed_tls_client_auth, RFC 8705 section 2) where client certificates are already managed.
claims.36-O2: A signed request object (RFC 9101), pushed through PAR, where the client must be able to prove afterwards what it requested.
claims.36-O3: Adopt the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile whole, with a certified implementation, where an ecosystem or a regulator requires it.

modules.title: SAML assertions and where they meet APIs

claims.37-S1: SAML V2.0 Profiles section 4.1.4.3 requires the service provider to verify any signatures present on the assertion or the response, to verify that the Recipient in the bearer confirmation data matches the assertion consumer service URL the response was delivered to, to verify that its NotOnOrAfter has not passed "subject to allowable clock skew between the providers", to verify that InResponseTo equals the ID of its original request unless the response is unsolicited, in which case the attribute must not be present, and to verify that any assertions relied upon are valid in other respects.
claims.37-S2: SAML V2.0 Profiles section 4.1.4.3 states these at lower strength. The service provider may check the client address against an Address attribute. An assertion that is not valid, or whose subject confirmation requirements cannot be met, should be discarded and should not be used to establish a security context. A session should be discarded at SessionNotOnOrAfter.
claims.37-S3: SAML V2.0 Profiles section 4.1.4.5, as reworded by the approved errata (E26, with the same change to section 4.1.3.5 in E93), requires for the HTTP POST binding that "each assertion MUST be protected by a digital signature", by signing each assertion or by signing the response. The same section requires the service provider to ensure that bearer assertions are not replayed, by keeping the set of used ID values for as long as the assertion would be considered valid from the NotOnOrAfter of its confirmation data.
claims.37-S4: SAML V2.0 Profiles section 4.1.4.2, as reworded by the approved errata (E26 and E52), requires the identity provider to put a bearer subject confirmation in the assertion, with a Recipient and a NotOnOrAfter, and requires each bearer assertion to contain an audience restriction naming the service provider. Section 4.1.4.1 requires the identity provider to verify that an assertion consumer service named in a request belongs to the service provider. Section 4.1.2 forbids the HTTP Redirect binding for the response.
claims.37-S5: SAML V2.0 Profiles section 4.1.5 allows an identity provider to send an unsolicited response, and requires that it contain no InResponseTo. The approved errata (E90) add that service providers should have a means of disabling the acceptance of unsolicited responses.
claims.37-S6: SAML V2.0 Core section 5.4.2 requires a signature to contain a single reference, to the ID of the root element of the assertion or message being signed. Section 5.4.1 requires enveloped signatures. Section 5.4.4 says signatures should not contain transforms other than the two it names, allows a verifier to reject others, and requires a verifier that does not to ensure that no content of the message is excluded from the signature. Section 5.4.5 neither requires <ds:KeyInfo> nor restricts it. Section 5.1 makes signing an assertion optional in general.
claims.37-S7: SAML V2.0 Core section 2.3.3 requires a relying party to verify a signature that is used, and says that if it is invalid the relying party "MUST NOT rely on the contents of the assertion". Section 2.5.1.1 requires a relying party to reject an assertion whose conditions are Invalid or Indeterminate. Section 2.5.1.4 says the audience restriction is Valid if and only if the relying party is a member of one of the audiences.
claims.37-S8: SAML V2.0 Bindings section 3.5.5.2 requires, when a message sent with the POST binding is signed, that its Destination hold the URL it was sent to and that the recipient verify it. Section 3.5.3 requires a RelayState value to be no longer than 80 bytes and says it should be integrity protected by its creator. The approved errata (E90) require implementations to sanitize the URL schemes they permit in RelayState.
claims.37-S9: The approved errata (E92) say SAML system entities should allow for reasonable clock skew and call 3 to 5 minutes reasonable defaults. E91 says <ds:Object> should not be present in a SAML signature and that verifiers should reject a signature that contains one.
claims.37-S10: RFC 7522 section 3 requires an authorization server that takes a SAML assertion as a grant to validate it: an issuer, an audience that identifies the authorization server (it "MUST reject any Assertion that does not contain its own identity as the intended audience"), a subject, an expiry, a bearer subject confirmation whose Recipient, when present, it must verify against the token endpoint, and a signature or MAC by the issuer. It allows replay protection and, in section 6, says the specification "does not mandate" it. Section 3.1 requires the error code invalid_grant for an assertion that is not valid.
claims.37-S11: RFC 8693 section 3 defines the token type identifier urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:saml2 for a base64url-encoded SAML 2.0 assertion. Section 2.1 requires the authorization server to perform the appropriate validation procedures for the indicated token type and leaves the criteria for any particular token out of scope.
claims.37-S12: The W3C note sets no requirements. It recommends that a verifier establish trust in the verification key (Best Practice 2), check both the name and the position of a referenced element (Best Practice 14), and that signers sign all parts of a document unless impractical (Best Practice 15) and not transmit unparsed external entity references (Best Practice 23).
claims.37-S13: The OWASP SAML Security Cheat Sheet sets no requirements. It recommends validating the document against local, trusted copies of schemas, obtaining the key directly from the identity provider and ignoring KeyInfo in the document, never selecting security elements with getElementsByTagName without prior validation, validating the audience, Recipient, InResponseTo and both time limits, implementing replay detection, and validating a RelayState URL against an allowlist. It calls unsolicited responses inherently less secure by design.
claims.37-B1: Read the user and every condition only from the assertion element that a verified signature covers. Never look the assertion up a second time.
claims.37-B2: Take the verification key from configuration, by issuer. Refuse an issuer with no configured key.
claims.37-B3: Refuse any message that contains a document type declaration, before parsing, and configure the parser to resolve nothing external.
claims.37-B4: Treat an invalid assertion as a refusal, although the profile says only that it should be discarded. Refuse unsolicited responses unless a named partner needs them.
claims.37-B5: Allow 180 seconds of clock skew. Keep used assertion IDs until the delivery window plus the skew has passed, in a store all servers share.
claims.37-B6: Send a random handle as RelayState and look the destination up in the session.
claims.37-B7: Create the service provider's own session and do not keep the assertion. No resource API accepts an assertion. An authorization server's token endpoint that takes one under RFC 7522 refuses a second use, although RFC 7522 only allows that.
claims.37-B8: Use a maintained SAML library with its strict options on, and run the negative tests in section 6 against it.
claims.37-O1: Accepting unsolicited responses from one identity provider, with the one-time cache in place and RelayState validated.
claims.37-O2: Requiring a signature on both the response and the assertion, where a partner's profile asks for it.
claims.37-O3: The RFC 7522 grant, or RFC 8693 token exchange with a SAML subject token, where no browser flow to the authorization server is possible.

packets.name: Core API and web application security

claims.00-S1: TLS authenticates the server by default and the client only if you configure it. "The server side of the channel is always authenticated; the client side is optionally authenticated." RFC 9846 section 1.
claims.00-S2: TLS protects the channel, not the stored data. The properties it lists are that data sent "after establishment is only visible to the endpoints" and "cannot be modified by attackers without detection". RFC 9846 section 1. Both end at the endpoints.
claims.00-S3: An HMAC is computed with a key shared by both parties, so verification capability equals production capability. RFC 2104 section 1 says message authentication codes "are used between two parties that share a secret key" and that HMAC "uses a secret key for calculation and verification". FIPS 198-1 section 1 says the same. Use HMAC as specified in RFC 2104 and FIPS 198-1. That is this page's advice: RFC 2104 is Informational and "does not specify an Internet standard of any kind".
claims.00-B1: Never treat a hash sent alongside the data it describes as integrity protection. Carry it inside something a key protects.
claims.00-B2: For every value in a request, be able to name who can produce it and who can check it, and record the answer where the design is written down.
claims.00-B3: Name the last TLS termination before your code, and treat everything past it as a separate trust relationship.
claims.00-B4: Authorize as a separate check, after authentication, naming the object. Never derive it from authentication having succeeded.
claims.00-B5: Place checks in the service that owns the data. Treat a gateway check as additional unless nothing else can reach the service.
claims.00-B6: Compare secrets and tags with a constant-time function. No functional test will catch the difference.
claims.00-O1: Use mutual TLS where you want the transport layer to carry caller identity, and confirm the certificate reaches the code that checks it rather than stopping at a proxy.

claims.09-S1: Object level authorization is "usually implemented at the code level to validate that a user can only access the objects that they should have permissions to access". OWASP API Security Top 10 2023, API1:2023.
claims.09-S2: Validate the caller's permission against every object reached using an identifier from client input, in every handler that reaches it. OWASP API1:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.09-S3: Write tests for the authorization mechanism and do not deploy a change that fails them. OWASP API1:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.09-S4: Prefer random, unpredictable values for record identifiers, such as GUIDs. OWASP API1:2023, How To Prevent. This raises the cost of discovery; it is not the access control.
claims.09-S5: A server may answer 404 in place of 403. RFC 9110 section 15.5.4 says an origin server that wishes to hide the current existence of a forbidden target resource "MAY instead respond with a status code of 404 (Not Found)", and section 15.5.5 says a 404 indicates that the origin server "did not find a current representation for the target resource or is not willing to disclose that one exists". The RFC allows either code, so choose the refusal code deliberately.
claims.09-B1: Load the object, read the owner from the loaded record, compare with the identity authentication produced, and refuse before any part of the response is built.
claims.09-B2: Never read the owner from a request parameter, header or body field.
claims.09-B3: Filter list endpoints in the query. Never after serialisation and never in the client.
claims.09-B4: Apply the check on every verb the object is exposed under, not only reads.
claims.09-B5: Give every related object its own check in its own handler. Reaching it through an object you own does not transfer ownership.
claims.09-B6: Return 404 for anything the caller may not see, consistently across the service.
claims.09-B7: Enumerate every path that reaches each object type, including older versions still serving traffic, and confirm each one carries the check.
claims.09-O1: Return 403 where the caller is entitled to know the object exists, such as a shared resource their access to was removed. Document it, and keep it out of the paths where existence is itself the secret.
claims.09-O2: Enforce ownership in the data access layer, so a handler that forgets the check cannot load the row at all. This trades some flexibility for a default that fails closed.

claims.10-S1: An endpoint is vulnerable where it "exposes properties of an object that are considered sensitive and should not be read by the user", or "allows a user to change, add/or delete the value of a sensitive object's property which the user should not be able to access". OWASP API3:2023, Is the API Vulnerable? The entry merges the 2019 edition's excessive data exposure and mass assignment categories.
claims.10-S2: "When exposing an object using an API endpoint, always make sure that the user should have access to the object's properties you expose." OWASP API3:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.10-S3: "Avoid using generic methods such as to_json() and to_string()." OWASP API3:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.10-S4: "If possible, avoid using functions that automatically bind a client's input into code variables", and "allow changes only to the object's properties that should be updated by the client". OWASP API3:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.10-S5: "Implement a schema-based response validation mechanism as an extra layer of security", and "keep returned data structures to the bare minimum, according to the business/functional requirements". OWASP API3:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.10-S6: "The enforcement mechanism(s) should deny all access by default, requiring explicit grants to specific roles for access to every function." OWASP API5:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.10-S7: "Don't assume that an API endpoint is regular or administrative only based on the URL path." OWASP API5:2023, Is the API Vulnerable? The same section notes it is "very common to find these administrative endpoints under other relative paths together with regular endpoints".
claims.10-B1: Declare two lists per endpoint, one readable and one writable, and build the response and the update from them rather than from the record.
claims.10-B2: Count and log the fields an update ignored, by name and never by value.
claims.10-B3: Key function rules by method and path together. A rule for GET says nothing about DELETE.
claims.10-B4: Refuse any request whose method and path have no rule, so a new endpoint is unreachable until somebody writes one.
claims.10-B5: Have somebody read the route table against what each operation does. Deny by default covers the routes nobody considered, not the rules somebody got wrong.
claims.10-B6: Keep the object check from module 9 on every one of these requests. Property and function checks say nothing about whose record it is.
claims.10-O1: Generate the response allowlist from the published API schema, so the contract and the filter cannot drift apart. This helps only if the schema is the source of truth rather than a document produced from the code.
claims.10-O2: Fail a build when a model gains a field that no endpoint's list mentions, which turns the silent version of this defect into a visible one.

claims.11-S1: A method is idempotent "if the intended effect on the server of multiple identical requests with that method is the same as the effect for a single such request". GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE are idempotent; POST is not. RFC 9110 section 9.2.2 for the definition, and the method table in section 18.2 for the list.
claims.11-S2: Identify the business flows that might harm the business if they are excessively used. OWASP API6:2023 says mitigation planning should be done in two layers and gives this as the first, the business layer, ahead of the engineering one.
claims.11-S3: OWASP API6:2023 describes the attack as "understanding the business model backed by the API, finding sensitive business flows, and automating access to these flows, causing harm to the business", with scalping, seat reservation and referral farming as its examples.
claims.11-B1: There is no standard for the Idempotency-Key header. draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header reached revision 07 in October 2025 and expired on 18 April 2026 without becoming an RFC. Treat the header as a convention, document your own semantics, and do not assume another service shares them.
claims.11-B2: Follow the expired draft's error behaviour, because each code names a distinct case: replay the stored response for a repeat of a completed request, 409 while a request with that key is in progress, 422 when the key arrives with a different payload.
claims.11-B3: Reserve the key before performing the operation, and store the response against it afterwards.
claims.11-B4: Store a fingerprint of the request payload with the key and compare it on every reuse.
claims.11-B5: Scope keys per caller and per operation type. Never a single global namespace.
claims.11-B6: Store and replay the original status and body, including failures. Do not recompute the response.
claims.11-B7: Keep keys for a documented period, 24 hours by default, and treat it as the outer bound on how late a retry can be recognised.
claims.11-B8: Log the idempotency key with each request, so duplicate execution and excessive use can be told apart from the data.
claims.11-B9: Enforce rate and quantity limits on the flow, across every endpoint that advances it, rather than per endpoint.
claims.11-O1: Model the operation as a PUT to a client-chosen identifier where the resource has a natural identity, which takes the idempotency from the method and needs no key at all.
claims.11-O2: Where a flow is valuable enough to attract automation, OWASP also lists device fingerprinting, human detection and non-human pattern analysis. These raise the cost of automation; they do not replace a limit.

claims.13-S1: RFC 8259 section 4 recommends, and does not require, unique names: "The names within an object SHOULD be unique." When they are not, it records three behaviours in use: "many implementations report the last name/value pair only. Other implementations report an error or fail to parse the object, and some implementations report all of the name/value pairs, including duplicates."
claims.13-S2: "Numeric values that cannot be represented in the grammar below (such as Infinity and NaN) are not permitted." RFC 8259 section 6.
claims.13-S3: RFC 8259 section 6 notes that "good interoperability can be achieved by implementations that expect no more precision or range than" IEEE 754 double precision provides, and that numbers implying more may indicate interoperability problems.
claims.13-S4: "A JSON parser MUST accept all texts that conform to the JSON grammar", and an implementation "may set limits on the size of texts that it accepts", "may set limits on the maximum depth of nesting" and "may set limits on the range and precision of numbers". RFC 8259 section 9. The limits are yours to set.
claims.13-S5: "Define and enforce a maximum size of data on all incoming parameters and payloads, such as maximum length for strings, maximum number of elements in arrays, and maximum upload file size". OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.13-S6: OWASP API4:2023 lists execution timeouts, maximum allocable memory, the number of operations in a single request and the number of records per page among the limits whose absence makes an API vulnerable.
claims.13-B1: Reject a body containing a repeated name. Do not resolve it.
claims.13-B2: Parse each request once, or prove that every component parsing it resolves the same bytes the same way.
claims.13-B3: Configure the parser to refuse NaN, Infinity and -Infinity.
claims.13-B4: Limit nesting depth to 64, measured from the text before parsing.
claims.13-B5: Enforce the decoded-size limit during decompression, stopping the decoder at the threshold, and bound the expansion ratio.
claims.13-B6: Give every numeric field an explicit range and every string and array field an explicit maximum length, per field rather than globally.
claims.13-B7: Return one status and a stable error shape naming the rule that refused the request, never echoing the offending value.
claims.13-O1: Do not accept compressed request bodies at all, which removes the decoded-size problem instead of bounding it.
claims.13-O2: Apply the same limits to responses you consume from other services, since a response is somebody else's body arriving at your parser.

claims.15-S1: "Implement a limit on how often a client can interact with the API within a defined timeframe (rate limiting)." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.15-S2: "Rate limiting should be fine tuned based on the business needs. Some API Endpoints might require stricter policies." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.15-S3: "Limit/throttle how many times or how often a single API client/user can execute a single operation (e.g. validate an OTP, or request password recovery without visiting the one-time URL)." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.15-S4: "Use a solution that makes it easy to limit memory, CPU, number of restarts, file descriptors, and processes such as Containers / Serverless code (e.g. Lambdas)." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.15-S5: "Configure spending limits for all service providers/API integrations. When setting spending limits is not possible, billing alerts should be configured instead." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.15-S6: "Define and enforce a maximum size of data on all incoming parameters and payloads, such as maximum length for strings, maximum number of elements in arrays, and maximum upload file size (regardless of whether it is stored locally or in cloud storage)." OWASP API4:2023, How To Prevent.
claims.15-S7: For applications built on language models, OWASP LLM06:2026 Unbounded Consumption recommends, in mitigation 1, Rate Limiting & Input Size Validation: "Apply rate limiting and user quotas to restrict the number of requests a single source entity can make in a given time period. Move beyond requests per second to enforce limits on tokens-per-minute, tokens-per-day, and estimated cost per request. Use pre-flight token estimation to reject requests before inference begins. This includes validation to ensure inputs do not exceed reasonable size limits." The tokens there are model tokens.
claims.15-S8: "Set non-overridable budget ceilings per API key, user, team, and cloud account. These must be enforcement mechanisms that halt inference when exceeded, rather than alerting thresholds that fast-accumulating workloads can outpace." OWASP LLM06:2026, mitigation 2, Hard Spending Caps. The word "must" is OWASP's, in a document that sets no requirements.
claims.15-S9: 429 Too Many Requests "indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time", the response "SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header", and responses with it "MUST NOT be stored by a cache". RFC 6585 section 4.
claims.15-S10: Servers "are not required to use the 429 status code; when limiting resource usage, it may be more appropriate to just drop connections, or take other steps", because responding to each request consumes resources. RFC 6585 section 7.2.
claims.15-B1: There is no standard for RateLimit response headers. draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers reached revision 11 in May 2026 and remains an Internet-Draft. Emit them if useful, and document them as yours.
claims.15-B2: Choose the algorithm by its worst moment, and write that number down beside the published limit.
claims.15-B3: Limit weighted cost rather than request count wherever operations differ by more than a small factor. For an API backed by a model, work the weight out for each request from its model tokens and a price table. OWASP LLM06:2026 recommends the same in mitigation 1, quoted above: limits on model tokens and on "estimated cost per request", beyond requests per second.
claims.15-B4: Publish a rate and a quota. The rate bounds a moment, the quota bounds a period. OWASP LLM06:2026, mitigation 1, recommends a per-minute and a per-day limit on model tokens in the passage quoted above.
claims.15-B5: For an endpoint backed by a model, cap the input size and the output a caller may ask for, and make every decision before the model is called. LLM06:2026 mitigation 1 names input size. The output cap is this project's addition: the entry's Description says the risk is compounded by reasoning models "with large or insufficiently constrained output budgets".
claims.15-B6: For an endpoint backed by a model, the budget ceiling for each caller or key is enforced: the call that would take the spend over it is refused, so the spend never passes it. An alert is an addition and never the control. OWASP API4:2023 accepts a billing alert where a spending limit cannot be set. For model spend this project does not, for the reason in section 2 and lab checks 39 to 43. Module 31 sets the same default for an agent run.
claims.15-B7: Hold counters in a store every instance shares, and test against a second instance rather than a second request.
claims.15-B8: State what the limit is per, and know the cost of obtaining another one of those.
claims.15-O1: Return Retry-After, defined in RFC 9110 section 10.2.3, on refusals where you want clients to back off predictably rather than retry immediately.
claims.15-O2: Drop rather than answer when the volume makes answering the expensive part. RFC 6585 permits this explicitly.

claims.17-S1: The CORS check reads Access-Control-Allow-Origin, fails if it is absent, succeeds on * only when credentials were not included, otherwise requires it to equal the request's byte-serialised origin, and when credentials were included additionally requires Access-Control-Allow-Credentials to be true. Fetch Standard section 4.10.
claims.17-S2: Access-Control-Allow-Credentials = %s"true" ; case-sensitive. True does not satisfy it. Fetch Standard section 3.3.4.
claims.17-S3: With credentials mode include, Access-Control-Allow-Origin cannot be *, and Access-Control-Expose-Headers, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers can only use * when credentials mode is not include. Fetch Standard section 3.3.5.
claims.17-S4: A serialised origin has no trailing slash, its scheme and domain are lower case ASCII without percent encoding, and this definition "supplants the definition in The Web Origin Concept". Fetch Standard section 3.2, and the table in section 3.3.5 for the trailing slash.
claims.17-S5: Authorization is the CORS non-wildcard request-header name, so Access-Control-Allow-Headers: * does not cover it, and a cached preflight entry stored as * does not match it. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.2, 4.8 and 4.9.
claims.17-S6: A request avoids a preflight only for a CORS-safelisted method, GET, HEAD or POST, with every header CORS-safelisted: no single safelisted value over 128 bytes, and the safelisted values together not over 1024 bytes. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2 for the definitions, and 4.1 for the preflight condition.
claims.17-S7: A safelisted Content-Type must parse to application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain, judged per header rather than through a forgiving extractor, so a server that reads a different duplicate than the browser judged is the hazard the standard warns about. Fetch Standard section 2.2.2.
claims.17-S8: A successful response to a preflight is restricted to an ok status; Access-Control-Max-Age is 5 seconds by default, and a value greater than an imposed limit is set to that limit. Fetch Standard sections 3.3.3 and 4.8.
claims.17-S9: Four non-safelisted Content-Type values are exempted from preflighting by other specifications: application/csp-report, application/expect-ct-report+json, application/xss-auditor-report and application/ocsp-request. Fetch Standard section 3.3.7.
claims.17-S10: The standard's informative background section says Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * is safe for a resource that could already be fetched by any device on the web, and that using CORS is unsafe for one protected by IP authentication or a firewall. Fetch Standard, Basic safe CORS protocol setup, under Background reading.
claims.17-B1: Hold an allowlist of exact serialised origins and compare byte for byte. Send the matched origin, or no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header at all.
claims.17-B2: Never construct the header from the request. Reflecting an unchecked origin allows every origin.
claims.17-B3: Send Vary: Origin on every response whose headers depend on the request's origin.
claims.17-B4: Set Access-Control-Max-Age deliberately, knowing the browser ceiling, and treat it as the delay before a tightened policy takes effect.
claims.17-B5: Assert the CORS response headers in tests, against allowed, disallowed and lookalike origins, rather than confirming the integration works in a browser console.
claims.17-B6: Protect state-changing endpoints with anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies. CORS does not stop the request arriving.
claims.17-O1: Serve the browser-facing API from the same origin through a reverse proxy, which removes the cross-origin question rather than configuring it.
claims.17-O2: Use a bearer token in Authorization rather than a cookie, so a cross-origin request carries no credential unless the page deliberately attaches one. Name the header in the preflight response.

claims.28-S1: A user agent that attaches a Cookie header must include a cookie with the Secure attribute only when the request uses a secure protocol, and must leave a cookie with HttpOnly out of the cookie string it builds for a non-HTTP API such as script access. Without a Domain attribute a cookie is host-only. RFC 6265 sections 5.3 and 5.4, summarized in sections 4.1.2.3 to 4.1.2.6.
claims.28-S2: Cookies are ambient authority: "user agents attach cookies even if the remote party does not know the contents of the cookies", which can let a remote party exercise authority at an unwary server. RFC 6265 section 8.2. This is the security considerations section and sets no requirement.
claims.28-S3: Safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE, and when a URL selects an unsafe action "the resource owner MUST disable or disallow that action when it is accessed using a safe request method". RFC 9110 section 9.2.1.
claims.28-S4: Draft: a user agent that attaches cookies must leave out a cookie whose same-site flag is not None when the request is cross-site, unless the flag is Lax or the default, the request is HTTP, the method is safe and the request's target is the active browsing context or a top-level traversable. The draft takes that term from the HTML Standard, and this page reads it as a tab or a window. draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22 sections 5.8.1 and 5.8.3. An Internet-Draft, not a standard.
claims.28-S5: Draft: a user agent must ignore a cookie with SameSite=None and no Secure, a cookie named __Secure- without Secure, and a cookie named __Host- unless it has Secure, no Domain and Path=/, matching the prefix without regard to case. Servers should use the prefixes. draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22 sections 5.7, 5.4 and 4.1.3.
claims.28-S6: Draft: Lax "does not offer a robust defense against CSRF as a general category of attack", and developers are strongly encouraged to deploy the usual server-side defences, for which it gives CSRF tokens and ensuring that safe methods are idempotent as examples. The server should take care to avoid session fixation. draft-ietf-httpbis-rfc6265bis-22 sections 5.6.7.1, 8.8.1 and 8.4.
claims.28-S7: A cross-origin request avoids a preflight when its method is GET, HEAD or POST and every header is CORS-safelisted, and a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain is safelisted. The Origin header is sent on CORS requests and on requests whose method is neither GET nor HEAD. Fetch Standard sections 2.2.1, 2.2.2, 3.2 and 4.1.
claims.28-S8: Working Draft: Sec-Fetch-Site carries cross-site, same-origin, same-site or none, where none marks a navigation the user caused directly. The Sec- prefix makes the header "unmodifiable from JavaScript". Servers should ignore the header if its value is invalid. Fetch Metadata Request Headers sections 2.3 and 4.2. A W3C Working Draft, not a Recommendation.
claims.28-S9: The CSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet recommends the synchronizer token pattern for stateful software and the signed double-submit cookie, bound to the session, for stateless software. It discourages the unsigned form, says a Fetch Metadata check needs a fallback to Origin or Referer verification, and says not to use GET for state-changing operations.
